newsitem.title: FRANCE: Prices up at annual French Burgundy charity sale.
newsitem.headline: Prices up at annual French Burgundy charity sale.

text.p: Burgundy wine prices held up well at the start of the annual Hospices de Beaune charity sale on Sunday but fell short of predictions prompted by the high quality of the 1996 vintage.
With more than half of the wine up for auction sold, the prices were up on average eight percent over 1995.

Before the auction began, trade specialists had predicted increases of between 10 and 20 percent. At last year's sale, prices rose 7.8 percent on average after soaring by more than 50 percent in 1994.
The auction, closely watched in wine circles around the world, provides a barometer of prices and the overall health of France's important wine trade.

Market professionals said prices failed to rise as much as expected because of high stocks available, a tough economic situation in France and a weak dollar which has made the wines more expensive internationally.
Burgundy Wine Board officials cautioned that consumers should not necessarily expect prices in wine shops to follow the trend set at the Beaune auction.
The auction was the earliest assessment of the market for the 1996 vintage, which was harvested just two months ago.

The wine-drinking public will have their first chance to sample the vintage on Thursday, when bottles of Beaujolais Nouveau from a region at the southern end of Burgundy are uncorked around the world amid much hype and celebration.
Burgundy wine board officials, who had pleaded publicly before Sunday's auction for moderation at the sale, said they were pleased by the price stability.

"For the moment I'm happy," said Louis Trebuchet, Burgundy wine board president. "It looks as though we're going to stay within the limits of the reasonable. The best thing for Burgundy and wine drinkers would be for great wine to be sold at stable prices."
"Nobody wants prices to go up and nobody wants prices to go down," Trebuchet said, striking a note of caution on Saturday. "We want a better link between quality and price."
Trebuchet said Burgundy's international reputation for sky-high prices and variable quality could be improved if prices remained less volatile in the years ahead.
Wine professionals said buyers taking advantage of the lower-than-expected prices were making some good deals.
Most agreed that cool, wet conditions in July and August combined with excellent weather during the harvest would produce wines with the greatest potential for some time.
"It's the best year since 1990," said one trade journalist with 15 years tasting the young wine out of huge oak barrels.
Trebuchet was more expansive, saying he believed the region had not produced such quantity with such consistent quality since 1959.

Average yields this year were about 30 percent higher than in 1995. But despite the increase, alcohol and acidity levels were high, color robust and tannins evident, indicating good potential for ageing, professionals said.

Proceeds from the auction after production costs go to the Hospices, built in 1443 by a tax collector for the king who, local legend has it, wanted to make up for some of his harsh tax-collecting practices over the years. The traditional auction dates from 1859 and has been held every third Sunday in November since 1924.
